title: Carpet to Hardwood Transitions: How Pros Finish the Edge
meta: Carpet to hardwood transitions done right: tack strip set back, carpet tucked into the gully, no metal strip unless heights differ. Wills Flooring, Edmonds.
keywords: carpet to hardwood transition, how to transition carpet to hardwood floor, carpet to wood floor transition strip, tuck carpet edge against hardwood, carpet hardwood doorway transition, carpet installation Edmonds

blocks.lead: A professional carpet-to-hardwood transition has no visible metal at all: the tack strip is set back from the hardwood by about the thickness of the carpet, the pad stops at the strip, and the carpet edge is stretched, trimmed and tucked down into that gully so it meets the wood as a clean, tight seam.
blocks.detail: Metal strips, Z-bars and wood reducers are for when the two floors sit at different heights or the carpet has to be held on a hard surface. In most Edmonds homes, where 3/4 in oak meets carpet over pad, the tuck is the right finish.

blocks.html: Walk through a 1960s Seaview or Westgate rambler and you will find the same detail at every bedroom door: a strip of gold or silver metal where the hallway oak meets the bedroom carpet, often bent, often with carpet fuzz pulling out of it. Homeowners assume that strip is required. It is not. It was the fast way to finish the edge, and it is the first thing we take out when we recarpet an Edmonds house. Here is how a good crew finishes that edge, and how to tell if yours was done right.

blocks.text: What is actually happening at the edge

items.title: The tack strip
items.text: A wood strip with angled pins, nailed to the subfloor parallel to the hardwood edge. Its job is to hold the carpet under tension. Where it sits decides everything: too close to the wood and there is no room to tuck; too far and the carpet edge sags into a gap.

items.title: The gully
items.text: The gap between the tack strip and the hardwood. It should be a little less than the carpet's thickness, usually around 1/4 to 3/8 in. The trimmed carpet edge is pushed down into it with a stair tool, so the cut edge disappears and the pile stands up flush against the wood.

items.title: The pad
items.text: Carpet cushion stops at the inside edge of the tack strip and is stapled there, never running under the strip or into the gully. Pad in the gully is why some transitions feel spongy and eventually let the carpet pull loose.

items.title: The trim cut
items.text: The carpet is stretched onto the pins first, then cut with a wall trimmer or knife leaving just enough to tuck. Cut short and the backing shows; cut long and the edge bunches up and wears. This is the step that separates a tight seam from a fuzzy one.

blocks.text: The four ways to finish the edge, and when each is right

No hardware. Carpet pile meets the wood edge in a straight line.

A thin metal lip pinches the carpet edge; nearly invisible when done well.

The visible metal strip most people picture. Durable but dated.

blocks.note: Each method can be done well or badly. The failures you see in older Edmonds homes are almost always bent binder bars and gullies cut too wide.

blocks.text: Where the transition goes, room by room

items.d: Bedroom doorways off a hardwood hall
items.text: The seam sits directly under the closed door, so from the hallway you see wood and from inside you see carpet. Hinge-side to latch-side, straight, not angled.
items.note: If the old metal strip left nail holes in the oak, we fill them before tucking.

items.d: Top of a carpeted staircase meeting a hardwood landing
items.text: The carpet wraps the top nosing and tucks to a tack strip on the landing side, or, on a hardwood landing, ends at a reducer. Never a metal bar at the top step; it is a trip point.
items.note: Common in Perrinville and Seaview split-entries.

items.d: Open living room to carpeted family room
items.text: With no door to hide under, the seam is placed at the narrowest point of the opening and kept perfectly straight. The carpet direction should run toward the opening so the pile does not show a shadow line.
items.note: We snap a line on the subfloor before the tack strip goes down.

items.d: Carpet meeting hardwood at a step-down
items.text: Where a 1970s sunken living room drops to carpet, the hardwood edge gets a stair nosing or bullnose and the carpet tucks beneath it. No metal, nothing to catch a toe.
items.note: Older Edmonds owners downsizing into ramblers ask about this one most.

blocks.text: When the tuck is the wrong choice

a.title: The clean tuck works when
items: Hardwood and carpet-plus-pad finish within about 1/4 in of each other
There is a wood subfloor to nail tack strip into
The carpet is a cut pile or dense loop with a stable backing
The edge is straight and under a door or at a natural room break

b.title: Choose a reducer or Z-bar when
items: The height difference is more than about 3/8 in; a tuck leaves a soft ledge
Carpet ends on concrete, tile or a slab where tack strip cannot go
A loose berber or wool loop is likely to unravel at a raw cut edge
A wheelchair or walker needs a smooth ramped edge, common in Edmonds retirement moves

blocks.title: Edmonds moisture note:
blocks.text: Homes in the Bowl and along the waterfront run higher humidity. Hardwood edges swell slightly in winter, so we leave the gully at the tighter end of the range in summer installs and never force a hardwood reducer hard against the carpet. A transition that is tight in August and loose in February was cut wrong.
Mistakes we fix in Edmonds houses every month

items.html: Metal binder bar at every door. It was standard in 1970s builder installs. Today it reads as a rental finish and the edges bend up over time. Replace it with a tuck when you recarpet.
Gully too wide. When the tack strip sits 3/4 in or more from the wood, the carpet edge has nothing to press against, sags, and the backing shows as a dark line.
Pad run under the tack strip. The strip floats, the pins lose bite and the carpet creeps back from the hardwood within a year.
Tack strip nailed into the hardwood. Some installers put the strip on the oak itself to close a gap. It splits the boards and ruins the edge for the next refinish.
Raw edge not sealed. On loop and wool carpets the cut edge should be glued or latex-sealed before tucking, or it frays at the door in months.
Sun-faded oak under the old strip. Pull a metal bar and you find a pale stripe where the wood never saw light. It blends only with a refinish of the hall, so plan both jobs together.

faq.q: Do you need a transition strip between carpet and hardwood?
faq.a: Not usually. When carpet over pad meets 3/4 in hardwood at roughly the same height, the professional finish is to tuck the carpet edge into a gully next to a tack strip, with no strip at all. A metal or wood transition is needed only when the two floors differ in height or the carpet ends on concrete or tile.

faq.q: Where should the carpet to hardwood transition be in a doorway?
faq.a: Directly under the door when it is closed. That way each room shows one floor. The seam should run straight from the hinge jamb to the latch jamb. In wide openings without a door, place it at the narrowest point and snap a line so it is perfectly straight.

faq.q: Why does my carpet edge pull away from the hardwood?
faq.a: Three common causes: the tack strip was set too far from the wood so the edge had nothing to press against, the pad was run under the strip so the pins lost their grip, or the carpet was never stretched properly before trimming. All three are installer errors and all three show up in older Edmonds homes.

faq.q: Can carpet be tucked against hardwood without a tack strip?
faq.a: No. The strip is what holds the carpet under tension at the edge. Gluing a carpet edge to the wood or subfloor is a temporary fix that fails and leaves adhesive on the oak. If there is no wood subfloor to nail into, a Z-bar or glue-down tack strip is used instead.

faq.q: Can you remove the old metal strips when you recarpet?
faq.a: Yes, and we recommend it. We pull the bar, fill the nail holes in the hardwood, set new tack strip at the correct setback and tuck the new carpet. If the wood under the old bar is lighter than the rest of the hall, only a refinish will blend it, so consider scheduling both.
